title: Vision Language Models are Biased
claim: State-of-the-art models give confidently wrong answers on simple objective visual tasks when the image resembles a familiar subject, answering with the prior instead of what is shown.
layout: Black title banner, then a list of 7 icon-tagged question prompts, then a 7-column table: one example image per domain (a–g), 5 model answer rows with ✗/✓, and Bias and GT rows below
description: A boxed figure with a black title banner reading 'Examples of VLM failures across 7 domains of VLMBias'. Below it, seven question prompts, each led by a small icon (animal, car logo, flag, chess piece, sudoku grid, glasses, dot grid), with the key word in bold, for example 'legs', 'stripes' and 'parallel'. The lower half is a table with seven columns labelled a–g. Each column has a thumbnail: a rooster, a Mercedes car, a US flag, a chess board, a sudoku grid, two lines in an optical illusion, and a dot grid. Five rows show model answers from Gemini-2.5 Pro, Sonnet-3.7, GPT-4.1, o3 and o4-mini, with the logo of each model at the left of its row. Nearly every answer carries a red ✗. A few green ✓ marks stand out. Below a divider, a 'Bias' row shows the expected stereotyped answer and a 'GT' row shows the ground truth. Rows alternate in gray shading, and the red and green marks draw the eye first.
caption: VLMs fail on 6 counting tasks (a--e & g) and one low-level vision task (f).
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) memorize a vast amount of prior knowledge from the Internet that helps them on downstream tasks but also may notoriously sway their outputs towards wrong or biased answers. In this work, we test how the knowledge about popular subjects hurt the accuracy of vision language models (VLMs) on standard, objective visual tasks of counting and identification. We find that state-of-the-art VLMs are strongly biased (e.g., unable to recognize the 4th stripe has been added to a 3-stripe Adidas logo) scoring an average of 17.05% accuracy in counting (e.g., counting stripes in an Adidas-like logo) across 7 diverse domains from animals, logos, chess, board games, optical illusions, to patterned grids. Removing image backgrounds nearly doubles accuracy (21.09 percentage points), revealing that contextual visual cues trigger these biased responses. Further analysis of VLMs' reasoning patterns shows that counting accuracy initially rises with thinking tokens, reaching ~40%, before declining with excessive reasoning. Our work presents an interesting failure mode in VLMs and a human-supervised automated framework for testing VLM biases. Code and data are available at: vlmsarebiased.github.io.
